comment: Biology multiple choice for modules 15-18 (Year 11: DNA and protein synthesis, inheritance, selection and evolution, genetic modification and cloning). Four options, answer is the 0-based index of the correct one.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is the genome of an organism?
options: All the DNA of the organism
The genes that code for enzymes
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The genome is the entire DNA of an organism — every chromosome, every gene.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is a gene?
options: A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein
A different version of an allele
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A gene is a section of a DNA molecule that codes for one specific protein.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Where in a human cell are the chromosomes found?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Chromosomes are in the nucleus, and genes are located on them.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which describes the structure of a DNA molecule?
options: One strand folded into a ball
Two strands coiled into a double helix
A single strand in a ring
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: DNA is two strands coiled to form a double helix, linked by paired bases.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which base pairs with adenine (A) in DNA?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: In DNA, A pairs with T and C pairs with G. Uracil is only found in RNA.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which base pairs with cytosine (C)?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: C always pairs with G.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What are the three parts of a nucleotide?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Each nucleotide is a sugar, a phosphate group and one of four bases.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: One strand of DNA reads TAC CGT. What is the complementary DNA strand?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Swap each base for its partner: T→A, A→T, C→G, G→C. DNA never contains U.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: RNA contains uracil (U) instead of thymine (T).

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which is a correct difference between DNA and RNA?
options: DNA is single-stranded; RNA is double-stranded
DNA contains ribose; RNA contains deoxyribose
DNA contains thymine; RNA contains uracil
DNA is short; RNA is very long
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: DNA: double-stranded, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: single-stranded, ribose, uracil.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Where does transcription take place?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Transcription — making mRNA from DNA — happens in the nucleus, where the DNA is.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is made during transcription?
options: A new copy of the chromosome
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Transcription copies the base sequence of a gene into messenger RNA.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is the mRNA made from the DNA strand ATTCCGAGT?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Pair each base (A→U, T→A, C→G, G→C). RNA has U, never T.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Where does translation take place?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Translation happens at the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is the job of tRNA in protein synthesis?
options: Carries the code out of the nucleus
Brings specific amino acids to the ribosome
Joins the two strands of DNA
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Each tRNA carries one specific amino acid to the ribosome. mRNA carries the code.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is a codon?
options: Three bases on mRNA that code for one amino acid
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A codon is a triplet of bases on mRNA. The matching triplet on tRNA is the anticodon.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Where is the anticodon found?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The anticodon is on tRNA and is complementary to a codon on mRNA.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which is the correct order for protein synthesis?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Transcription copies DNA into RNA; translation turns the RNA code into protein.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: How many bases code for one amino acid?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The code is read in triplets — three bases per amino acid.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: A section of mRNA is 90 bases long. How many amino acids does it code for?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: 90 ÷ 3 = 30. Each codon of three bases codes for one amino acid.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Why is mRNA needed to make proteins?
options: Amino acids are only found in the nucleus
DNA stays in the nucleus but proteins are made at ribosomes in the cytoplasm
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: mRNA is a mobile copy of the gene that carries the code from the nucleus to the ribosomes.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: During translation, what joins to the mRNA codon?
options: The anticodon of a tRNA molecule
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A tRNA with a complementary anticodon binds to the codon and delivers its amino acid.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What happens to the amino acids brought to the ribosome?
options: They are joined into a chain — a polypeptide
They are broken down for energy
They are stored in the nucleus
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The amino acids are joined in the order set by the codons, forming a polypeptide that folds into a protein.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What decides the shape of a protein?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The order of amino acids decides how the chain folds, and so the protein's shape.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is a mutation?
options: A rare, random change in the base sequence of DNA
A change in the number of ribosomes
A new combination of alleles at fertilisation
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A mutation is a rare, random change in genetic material, which can be inherited.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: A mutation changes one codon so that a different amino acid is added. What is the most likely result for an enzyme?
options: The active site may change shape so the substrate no longer fits
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A different amino acid can change the folding and so the shape of the active site.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which statement about mutations is correct?
options: Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Most mutations have no effect, some have a small effect, and only rarely is the effect significant.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Why might a change in one base have no effect on the protein?
options: The new codon may code for the same amino acid
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Many amino acids have more than one codon, so the amino acid — and the protein — can stay the same.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: A person has one mutated allele of a gene but no symptoms. What is the most likely reason?
options: The mutation is in a ribosome
The mutation made the gene longer
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A recessive allele is not expressed while a dominant, working allele is present.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which of these increases the rate of mutation?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Ionising radiation — gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet — increases the incidence of mutations.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which is a chemical mutagen?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Some chemicals, such as those in tobacco, increase the rate of mutation.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which type of radiation is NOT ionising?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Gamma, X-rays and UV are ionising and can cause mutations. Radio waves are not.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Where do new alleles come from?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Mutation is the only source of brand-new alleles. Meiosis and fertilisation shuffle existing ones.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: An amino acid has 4 codons, a second has 2 and a third has 1. How many mRNA sequences could code for all three in that order?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Multiply the choices: 4 × 2 × 1 = 8.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which structure is the site of protein synthesis?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Proteins are assembled at ribosomes during translation.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: During transcription, which base in the mRNA pairs with adenine on the DNA?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: RNA has no thymine, so uracil pairs with adenine.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which row is correct for translation?
options: Codon on tRNA, anticodon on mRNA
Codon on mRNA, anticodon on tRNA
Codon on DNA, anticodon on mRNA
Codon on tRNA, anticodon on DNA
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The codon is on mRNA; the complementary anticodon is on tRNA.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: How does a gene affect a characteristic such as eye colour?
options: The gene itself is the colour
The gene moves to the eye
The gene is made of pigment
It codes for a protein, which affects the characteristic
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A gene codes for a protein — often an enzyme — and the protein produces the characteristic.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Beta thalassaemia is caused by a mutation in a haemoglobin gene. Why do people with it tire quickly?
options: Less haemoglobin means less oxygen carried, so less respiration in muscles
Their lungs cannot take in air
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Less working haemoglobin carries less oxygen, so less aerobic respiration and less energy released.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Near a radioactive leak, more abnormal butterflies are found. Why can't scientists be certain the radiation caused them?
options: There is no control group or data from before the leak
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Without a control or earlier data, the normal level of abnormality is unknown, and other factors could be responsible.

16-inheritance.q: What is an allele?
options: A different form of the same gene
16-inheritance.explain: Alleles are alternative versions of a gene, which cause differences in inherited characteristics.

16-inheritance.q: What is meant by a dominant allele?
options: It is the most common allele
It is stronger than other alleles
It is only expressed with two copies
Only one copy is needed for it to be expressed in the phenotype
16-inheritance.explain: A dominant allele is expressed even when only one copy is present. It is not necessarily common.

16-inheritance.q: What is meant by a recessive allele?
options: Only expressed when two copies are present
16-inheritance.explain: A recessive allele is only expressed when no dominant allele is present — two copies.

16-inheritance.q: Which genotype is heterozygous?
16-inheritance.explain: Heterozygous means two different alleles.

16-inheritance.q: Which genotype is homozygous recessive?
16-inheritance.explain: Homozygous recessive means two identical recessive alleles.

16-inheritance.q: What is the phenotype of an organism?
16-inheritance.explain: Phenotype is what you can observe; genotype is the combination of alleles.

16-inheritance.q: Which is a genotype?
16-inheritance.explain: Genotypes are written as alleles. The others are phenotypes.

16-inheritance.q: An organism shows the recessive characteristic. What is its genotype?
16-inheritance.explain: A recessive phenotype can only come from two recessive alleles.

16-inheritance.q: An organism shows the dominant characteristic. What could its genotype be?
16-inheritance.explain: BB and Bb look the same, because one dominant allele is enough.

16-inheritance.q: How many alleles of each gene does a gamete carry?
16-inheritance.explain: Gametes are made by meiosis and carry one chromosome of each pair, so one allele of each gene.

16-inheritance.q: What gametes can a parent with genotype Hh produce?
16-inheritance.explain: Each gamete gets one allele, so half carry H and half carry h.

16-inheritance.q: Hh is crossed with hh. What is the expected ratio of offspring phenotypes?
16-inheritance.explain: The offspring are Hh, Hh, hh, hh — half show the dominant characteristic.

16-inheritance.q: Two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) are crossed. What is the expected ratio of phenotypes?
16-inheritance.explain: AA, Aa, Aa, aa: three show the dominant characteristic, one the recessive. 1 : 2 : 1 is the genotype ratio.

16-inheritance.q: Two parents are Aa × Aa. What is the probability of an aa child?
16-inheritance.explain: One of the four equally likely outcomes is aa: 1/4 = 0.25.

16-inheritance.q: Two parents are Aa × Aa. What is the probability of a heterozygous child?
16-inheritance.explain: Two of the four boxes are Aa: 2/4 = 0.5.

16-inheritance.q: AA is crossed with aa. What are the offspring?
16-inheritance.explain: One parent can only give A and the other only a, so every offspring is Aa.

16-inheritance.q: Black rats are crossed with agouti rats and all the offspring are agouti. What does this show?
16-inheritance.explain: The offspring carry both alleles but only agouti shows, so agouti is dominant.

16-inheritance.q: Two unaffected parents have a child with a genetic condition. What does this show?
options: The condition is recessive and both parents are carriers
Only the mother carries the allele
The child has a new mutation in every cell
16-inheritance.explain: The child must be homozygous recessive, so each unaffected parent must be heterozygous.

16-inheritance.q: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. Two carriers have a child. What is the chance the child has cystic fibrosis?
16-inheritance.explain: Ff × Ff gives 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff, so 1 in 4.

16-inheritance.q: Two carriers already have one child with cystic fibrosis. What is the chance their next child has it?
16-inheritance.explain: Each fertilisation is independent. The chance stays 1 in 4 for every child.

16-inheritance.q: What is the probability of a child being male?
16-inheritance.explain: Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y; eggs all carry X.

16-inheritance.q: What are the sex chromosomes of a human male?
16-inheritance.explain: Females are XX and males are XY.

16-inheritance.q: Which gamete decides the sex of a child?
16-inheritance.explain: Every egg carries X. A sperm carries X or Y, so the sperm decides.

16-inheritance.q: Aa × Aa, where A is dominant. What is the probability of a child that is male AND shows the dominant characteristic?
16-inheritance.explain: Multiply: P(male) × P(dominant) = 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8 = 0.375.

16-inheritance.q: Two roan cattle (CRCW) are mated. What is the probability of a male roan calf?
Two parents are Ff × Ff. What is the probability that their next two children both have the recessive condition?
16-inheritance.explain: Each child independently has a 1/4 chance: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

16-inheritance.q: What does codominance mean?
options: The alleles are on different chromosomes
Both alleles are expressed in the phenotype
16-inheritance.explain: With codominance, the heterozygote shows both alleles — like roan cattle or blood group AB.

16-inheritance.q: Red cattle (CRCR) are crossed with white cattle (CWCW). The alleles are codominant. What are the calves?
16-inheritance.explain: Every calf is CRCW, and with codominance that is roan.

16-inheritance.q: Two roan cattle are mated. What is the expected ratio of calves?
16-inheritance.explain: CRCW × CRCW gives CRCR, CRCW, CRCW, CWCW — red, roan, roan, white.

16-inheritance.q: Parents have blood group genotypes IAIO and IBIO. Which blood groups could their children have?
16-inheritance.explain: The four boxes are IAIB (AB), IAIO (A), IBIO (B) and IOIO (O).

16-inheritance.q: Which person has blood group O?
16-inheritance.explain: IO is recessive, so group O needs two IO alleles.

16-inheritance.q: In a pedigree diagram, what does a shaded circle usually show?
16-inheritance.explain: Circles are females and squares are males; shading shows the condition.

16-inheritance.q: A person with a recessive condition (ff) has a child with an unaffected person. The child is unaffected. What is the child's genotype?
16-inheritance.explain: The child must have received f from the affected parent, but is unaffected, so is Ff.

16-inheritance.q: A cross gives 608 plants with one characteristic and 250 with the other. What is the ratio in the form n : 1?
Why does a cross expected to give 3 : 1 rarely give exactly 3 : 1?
options: Which gametes fuse at fertilisation is random
16-inheritance.explain: A ratio is a probability. Chance decides which gametes meet, so real numbers vary around it.

16-inheritance.q: How could a breeder find out whether a black dog is BB or Bb (black dominant)?
options: Breed it with a brown dog (bb) and look for brown puppies
Breed it with another BB dog
Look at its fur more closely
16-inheritance.explain: Any brown puppy must have received b from the black parent, proving it is Bb.

16-inheritance.q: What is polygenic inheritance?
options: A characteristic controlled by many genes
16-inheritance.explain: Polygenic means many genes. Most characteristics, such as height, are polygenic.

16-inheritance.q: Why is there a wider range of heights in a herd of cattle than hair colours?
options: Hair colour is affected by diet
Height is controlled by one gene
Height is polygenic and also affected by the environment
16-inheritance.explain: Many genes each add a little to height, and nutrition affects it too, so there is a smooth range.

16-inheritance.q: Why is a harmful recessive allele harder for breeders to remove than a dominant one?
options: It is hidden in heterozygous carriers that look normal
16-inheritance.explain: Carriers show no sign, so they are bred from and pass the allele on unnoticed.

16-inheritance.q: How can you tell from a karyotype that a person is male?
options: The 23rd pair is one X and one smaller Y
16-inheritance.explain: Males are XY, so the sex chromosome pair is unmatched — one large X, one small Y.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which of these is an example of variation caused only by the environment?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: A scar comes from an injury during life, not from alleles.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which characteristic is affected by both genes and the environment?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Genes set a range of possible heights; diet and health decide where in it a person ends up.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which is the only source of brand-new alleles?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Meiosis and fertilisation shuffle existing alleles; mutation creates new ones.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which of these does NOT produce genetic variation?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells, so it gives no variation.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Identical twins raised apart differ in body mass. What causes the difference?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Identical twins have identical alleles, so any difference must be environmental.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Whose theory explains evolution by natural selection?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Charles Darwin proposed evolution by natural selection.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What is the first step in natural selection?
options: A mutation produces variation in the population
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Variation must exist first — new alleles arise by random mutation.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: In natural selection, what is passed on to the offspring?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: The mark scheme wants alleles or genes. 'Passes on the mutation' or 'behaviour' alone did not score.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which is the correct order of natural selection?
options: Variation → survive → reproduce → pass on alleles
Reproduce → variation → pass on alleles → survive
Pass on alleles → survive → variation → reproduce
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Mutation gives variation; the best suited survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why are individuals with an advantageous characteristic more likely to pass on their alleles?
options: They are more likely to survive and reproduce
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Surviving to breed is what lets an allele reach the next generation.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Some woodlice roll into a ball when touched. How does this give a survival advantage?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Rolling up exposes only the hard outer shell, so they are less likely to be eaten.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which statement about adaptation by natural selection is correct?
options: Individuals change during their lives to suit the environment
The population changes over many generations
Organisms learn new features and pass them on
Features used a lot become inherited
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Individuals do not change; the proportion of alleles in the population changes over generations.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What is evolution?
options: A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time
Growth of an organism during its life
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Evolution is a change in inherited characteristics over many generations.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: When have two populations become separate species?
options: When they live in different places
When they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Separate species cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Giant whales are thought to have replaced the shark megalodon. Which idea best explains this?
options: The whales mutated to become sharks
The whales were better adapted, so they won the competition for food
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Competition for the same food: the better-adapted whales survived and reproduced more.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: How do bacteria first become resistant to an antibiotic?
options: They absorb resistance from the patient
A random mutation produces a resistance allele
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: The resistance allele comes from a random mutation. The antibiotic only selects it.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What does the antibiotic do in the development of resistance?
options: Kills the non-resistant bacteria, leaving resistant ones to multiply
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: It removes the competition, so the resistant bacteria survive and reproduce.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why does antibiotic resistance spread so quickly?
options: Bacteria reproduce very quickly, so there are many generations
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Bacteria can divide every 20 minutes or so, so selection happens over many generations quickly.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What is MRSA?
options: A strain of bacteria resistant to many antibiotics
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: MRSA is a strain of Staphylococcus aureus resistant to many antibiotics.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why should antibiotics not be prescribed for a cold?
options: Colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not kill
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Antibiotics do not affect viruses. Using them anyway selects for resistant bacteria.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why are patients told to finish a course of antibiotics?
options: To stop them catching a virus
To kill all the bacteria, including the more resistant ones
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Stopping early can leave the more resistant bacteria alive to multiply.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why are resistant infections difficult to control?
options: The antibiotic no longer kills the bacteria, so they keep spreading
Resistant bacteria cannot be passed between people
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: The usual antibiotic fails, so the bacteria keep multiplying and spreading.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Fire ant numbers fall after pesticide, then rise again. Which explanation uses natural selection?
options: The ants learned to avoid the pesticide
The pesticide caused mutations in all the ants
Resistant ants survived, reproduced and passed on the resistance allele
The ants moved away and came back
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: A few ants already had a resistance allele; they survived and bred.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Who chooses which individuals reproduce in selective breeding?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: In selective breeding, humans pick the parents with the characteristic they want.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which is the correct sequence for selective breeding?
options: Breed any two parents once and keep all offspring
Select parents, breed, select best offspring, repeat over many generations
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: The key words are select, breed, select the offspring, and repeat over many generations.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which is an example of selective breeding?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: High-yield wheat was produced by humans choosing and crossing the best plants over generations.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why is dwarf wheat useful to farmers?
options: It is resistant to all diseases
It grows taller and catches more light
Less energy goes into the stem, so more into grain, and it is less likely to fall over
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: A short, thick stem means more energy for grain and less damage from wind and rain.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which characteristic might a farmer selectively breed for in dairy cows?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Dairy farmers select cows that give the most milk.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What is the main disadvantage of selective breeding?
options: It is faster than natural selection
It increases the number of alleles
It reduces variation, making the population vulnerable to disease
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Breeding from a few related individuals narrows the range of alleles.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What is inbreeding?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Inbreeding means breeding related individuals, which increases the chance of genetic disorders.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why does inbreeding increase genetic disorders?
options: Related parents are more likely to carry the same harmful recessive allele
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Two carriers of the same recessive allele are more likely to meet, producing homozygous recessive offspring.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: How is natural selection different from selective breeding?
options: In natural selection the environment determines which individuals survive
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Nature selects for survival; humans select for features useful to them.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What do natural selection and selective breeding have in common?
options: Both need variation and change allele frequency over generations
Both are carried out by humans
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Both act on existing variation, over many generations.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why does selective breeding of fish for fast growth work?
options: Alleles for fast growth are passed on to the offspring
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Breeding the fastest growers means their alleles for fast growth are passed on and become more common.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why does cattle height vary over a smooth range while hair colour has only three types?
options: Hair colour is affected by diet
Height is polygenic and affected by the environment
Height is controlled by one gene
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Many genes plus the environment give a continuous range; one gene gives a few clear types.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: A field of genetically very similar wheat is wiped out by a new disease. Why?
options: Little variation — no plants had an allele to resist it
The disease was caused by selective breeding
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Low genetic variation means no individuals are likely to be resistant.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Wheat yield rose from 2.8 to 6.7 tonnes per hectare. What is the percentage increase?
Hares with white fur are more common where there is snow for most of the year. Which explanation is correct?
options: Hares turn white because they are cold
White hares are camouflaged, so survive and reproduce more, passing on alleles for white fur
Snow causes mutations for white fur
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: The advantage — camouflage from predators — means more white hares survive to breed.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why is only genetic variation important for natural selection?
options: Only genetic variation can be inherited by offspring
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Selection changes the next generation only through alleles passed on in gametes.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which of these helps slow the spread of antibiotic resistance?
options: Stopping a course as soon as you feel better
Using the same antibiotic for everything
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Hygiene stops resistant bacteria spreading between patients.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: What is genetic modification?
options: Breeding the best animals over many generations
Inserting a gene from one organism into another
Making identical copies of an organism
Changing the environment of an organism
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Genetic modification moves a gene from one organism into the DNA of another.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: What does 'transgenic' mean?
options: Containing a gene from a different species
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: A transgenic organism has genetic material transferred from a different species.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which enzyme cuts DNA at a specific base sequence?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Restriction enzymes cut; ligase joins.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: What does DNA ligase do?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Ligase joins the backbones of DNA, sealing the gene into the plasmid.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: What are 'sticky ends'?
options: Short unpaired sections of DNA that can pair with complementary ends
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Restriction enzymes leave single-stranded ends that base-pair with complementary sticky ends.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Why is the same restriction enzyme used to cut the gene and the plasmid?
options: To give complementary sticky ends that can pair up
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: The same enzyme cuts the same sequence, so the sticky ends match.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: What is a plasmid?
options: A small ring of DNA in a bacterium
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Plasmids are small, circular pieces of DNA separate from the bacterial chromosome.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which two can act as vectors in genetic modification?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: A vector carries the gene into a cell. Plasmids and viruses both do this.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: What is recombinant DNA?
options: DNA combined from two different organisms
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: A plasmid carrying a human gene is recombinant DNA.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which is the correct order for making GM bacteria that produce insulin?
options: Ligase cuts gene → restriction enzyme joins → plasmid into bacterium
Cut gene and plasmid with restriction enzyme → join with ligase → plasmid into bacterium
Plasmid into bacterium → cut gene → join with ligase
Cut plasmid with ligase → insert into human cell → join with restriction enzyme
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Cut both with the same restriction enzyme, join with ligase, then put the plasmid into a bacterium.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Where are GM bacteria grown to produce large amounts of insulin?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Industrial fermenters give the bacteria nutrients and ideal conditions to multiply.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Why can bacteria make human insulin from a human gene?
options: The genetic code is the same in all organisms
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Bacterial ribosomes read the human codons exactly as human cells would.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which is an advantage of insulin made by GM bacteria?
options: It is a different shape from human insulin
It can only be made in small amounts
It is identical to human insulin and made in large amounts
It needs pigs to be produced
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: It matches human insulin and bacteria multiply rapidly, so large amounts are made.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which enzyme is used to remove a gene from a section of DNA?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: A restriction enzyme cuts the gene out. Ligase was the tempting wrong answer on the 2022 paper.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: How does a pest-resistant GM crop increase yield?
options: It makes a toxin that kills insects eating it, so less crop is lost
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Fewer insects eat the crop, so more is harvested and less insecticide is needed.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: How does a herbicide-resistant crop increase yield?
options: The crop makes its own fertiliser
The crop photosynthesises twice as fast
Weeds can be sprayed without harming the crop, reducing competition
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: With fewer weeds, the crop has more light, water and mineral ions.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which is a concern about growing GM crops?
options: The new gene could spread to wild plants by pollination
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Pollen could carry the gene to wild relatives, e.g. producing herbicide-resistant weeds.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: What is a clone?
options: An organism with a gene from another species
A genetically identical copy of an organism
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Clones have identical DNA.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which type of cell division produces clones?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Mitosis copies chromosomes exactly. Meiosis was rejected by the 2024 mark scheme.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: What is micropropagation?
options: Growing many plant clones from small pieces of tissue on agar
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Micropropagation, or tissue culture, grows explants on agar with nutrients and hormones.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: In micropropagation, why are the explants sterilised?
options: To kill microorganisms that would compete with or infect them
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Microbes would thrive on the nutrient agar and harm the tiny plant pieces.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which substances are added to the agar in micropropagation?
options: Glucose, mineral ions and plant hormones such as auxin
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: The explants need nutrients and hormones to divide and grow roots and shoots. 'Nutrients' alone was ignored.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which part of a plant is often used for micropropagation?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Small pieces from actively growing tissue, such as shoot tips, are used.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Why is micropropagation used to copy a single transgenic plant?
options: It needs a second plant for pollination
It produces large numbers of identical plants quickly
It makes the plants grow faster
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: All the copies carry the new gene, many are made fast, and no mate is needed.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which is a disadvantage of micropropagation?
options: It can only be done in summer
The plants have no variation, so one disease could kill them all
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Clones share the same alleles, so none may resist a new disease.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: In cloning Dolly the sheep, what was removed from the egg cell?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: The egg was enucleated — its own nucleus removed.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Where did the nucleus inserted into the egg come from, when cloning Dolly?
options: An adult body cell of the sheep being cloned
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: A diploid nucleus from a mature body cell (an udder cell) was used.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: What makes the cloned egg cell start dividing?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: An electric shock stimulates the cell to divide into an embryo.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Where does the cloned embryo develop?
options: In the uterus of a surrogate mother
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: The embryo is implanted into a surrogate's uterus.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: A clone is made using a body cell from a black sheep, an egg from a white sheep and a brown surrogate. What colour is the lamb?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: All the lamb's chromosomes come from the black sheep's body-cell nucleus.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Why is a body-cell nucleus used for cloning rather than a sperm nucleus?
options: A body cell is diploid — it has the full set of chromosomes
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Gametes are haploid and each has a different mix of alleles.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which is the correct order for cloning a mammal?
options: Electric shock → remove egg nucleus → implant → insert body-cell nucleus
Insert body-cell nucleus → remove egg nucleus → shock → implant
Remove egg nucleus → insert body-cell nucleus → electric shock → implant embryo
Implant egg → remove nucleus → electric shock → insert nucleus
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Enucleate the egg, insert the body-cell nucleus, shock it to divide, implant the embryo.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: How are cloned transgenic animals used to produce human proteins?
options: Their meat is turned into insulin
They are cloned from human cells
A human gene is added so the protein is made in their milk, then the animal is cloned
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Cloning the transgenic animal gives a herd that all make the protein.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Why clone a transgenic goat rather than breed from it?
options: Every clone carries the gene, whereas only some offspring of breeding would
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Sexual reproduction mixes in a mate's alleles, so not every offspring inherits the gene.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Which is an argument FOR cloning animals?
options: Many identical animals with a valuable feature can be produced
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Cloning copies a valuable animal exactly. It has a low success rate and no variation.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Scientists want to use frozen cells to clone an extinct mammoth. Which cell would provide the egg?
options: An egg from a living related species, such as an elephant
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: No mammoth eggs exist, so an egg from a related living species would be enucleated and used.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: GM fish grow faster and waste less food. Which point supports the claim that farming them is better for the environment?
options: Escaped GM fish could breed with wild fish
Less waste means less decomposition, so more oxygen stays in the water
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Less waste food and faeces means fewer decomposers using oxygen and less eutrophication. The other options are points against.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Why might GM crops lead to less insecticide being used?
options: The crop makes its own insecticide
Insecticides stop working on GM crops
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: Pest-resistant crops make a toxin, so less spraying is needed.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: Golden Rice has been genetically modified to…
options: make a substance the body converts into vitamin A
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: It improves diet where rice is the main food.

18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.q: In the insulin process, what is the bacterial plasmid acting as?
18-genetic-modification-and-cloning.explain: A vector carries the gene into the host cell.
